issues.legal_issue: A murder conviction cannot be sustained on evidence that is rejected as to the alleged fatal assailant when the accused’s own act causing the fatal injuries is not proved and constructive liability is unavailable.
material_facts: The accused was convicted of murder after the High Court acquitted his brother, whom the eyewitnesses identified as inflicting the fatal blows.

The High Court relied on the same eyewitnesses to convict the accused, although their account attributed to him the act of restraining the deceased and did not establish which part of the deceased he struck.
The Supreme Court considered the eyewitness account unreliable against the accused in light of its rejection as to the other accused and found no evidence that the accused caused the fatal injuries.
issues.conclusion: The murder conviction could not be sustained: after the alleged fatal assailant was acquitted, constructive liability was unavailable on these facts, and there was no evidence that the accused caused the fatal injuries. The conviction was set aside and the accused was acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 and 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, substantive murder liability requires evidence that the accused caused the fatal injuries, while constructive liability under Section 34 depends on the basis established for shared participation. On these facts, the acquittal of the alleged fatal assailant left no scope for applying Section 34, and the rejected eyewitness account could not sustain a conviction of the remaining accused. Suspicion cannot take the place of proof. No earlier cases are cited.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a murder conviction, the alleged fatal assailant is acquitted, the eyewitness account about that assailant is discredited, and the accused is not proved to have caused the fatal injuries, the murder conviction cannot be sustained.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for causing disappearance of evidence cannot be sustained when it rests substantially on evidence of the main incident that the court has rejected and the remaining circumstances do not establish the offence.
material_facts: The accused was also convicted of causing disappearance of evidence in connection with the deceased’s body being put in a bag and taken to a tank.
The Supreme Court found that the evidence against the accused concerning this offence was substantially the same as the evidence concerning the murder charge.
The court rejected the direct evidence concerning the main assault and held that the circumstances relied on by the State were of no consequence once that evidence was disbelieved.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for causing disappearance of evidence could not be sustained and was set aside; the accused was acquitted of that charge.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 201 of the Indian Penal Code, a conviction cannot stand where the evidence against the accused on that offence is substantially the same as evidence rejected concerning the main incident, and the remaining circumstances do not sustain the charge. The court held that the State’s circumstances were of no consequence after the direct evidence was disbelieved. No earlier cases are cited.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a disappearance-of-evidence conviction, the supporting evidence substantially matches discredited evidence about the main incident, and the remaining circumstances do not sustain the charge, the conviction cannot be sustained.
